Compounded Wegovy and Zepbound: Legitimate or Risky?

What Are Compounding Pharmacies?
Compounding pharmacies have a long history, originally creating customized medications based on doctors' prescriptions. Today, they’re specialized labs that modify medications for patients' needs, like altering a drug’s form or taste. Importantly, they also make medications that are in short supply. Currently, Wegovy (semaglutide) is still on the FDA's shortage list, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) is not.

Why the Demand?
When the FDA approved Ozempic for diabetes in 2017 and Wegovy for weight loss in 2021, demand quickly skyrocketed. Social media boosted interest, creating shortages and making compounded versions popular and affordable alternatives. Compounding pharmacies stepped in to help meet demand.

The Controversy
The main concern is safety and effectiveness. Compounded versions aren’t the same as FDA-approved drugs because compounding pharmacies don't use the original patented formula. The FDA issued warnings, especially about potential dosing errors. Unlike FDA-approved drugs that come in single-dose pens, compounded medications often require patients to measure doses themselves, increasing the risk of errors.
Another issue is the quality control difference between types of pharmacies. Larger compounding facilities (known as “503b”) follow strict FDA federal oversight guidelines, while smaller pharmacies (known as "503a" pharmacies) follow the State boards of pharmacy do not face the same requirements. This can lead to inconsistencies in the final product.

What You Need to Know
· Safety and Efficacy Concerns: Compounded weight loss drugs don’t match the quality standards of FDA-approved versions.
· Regulatory Warnings: Leading obesity organizations and the FDA have cautioned against using compounded weight loss drugs.
· Availability Limits: Compounded Zepbound is no longer allowed, as it’s off the shortage list. Wegovy remains on the list, allowing compounded versions.

So, What Should You Do?
Talk with your doctor about the best option for you. If your insurance doesn't cover FDA-approved medications or if the cost is too high, discuss compounded alternatives—but keep FDA warnings in mind. Working with a doctor who understands the authorization process may improve your chances of insurance coverage for approved medications.

Ahead of the results, analysts had been concerned that lower pricing and muted prescriptions would hurt sales of the drug in the quarter, while disappointing obesity sales last week from Eli Lilly had heightened fears.

Next couple of years is a long timeframe though.

The potential of this drug is pretty strong but I personally believe many overestimate it, although it is of course better to keep it than not. Those who have been following me also know that I in general would prefer the market didn’t see these short P1 4w data with very few patients per arm. Theres an element of “coincidence” where just 1-2 patients can skew the whole data. Also, the base data jumps a lot with up to 4 point BMI difference between the groups as well as the split between women and men. So its easy to “overanalyze” short/small P1 studies.

With that said, below are my thoughts on the new oral vk2735 data.

We already knew the 40mg data. Topline was 5.1% WL (3.7% placebo adjusted)

60mg dropped to 4.1% (2.7% placebo adjusted)

80mg was 5.2% (4.1% placebo adjusted)

Overall double the dose but the same WL.

100mg did hit the magical 8.1% (6.8% placebo adjusted)

It’s actual the 100mg that’s the outlier. And I would be careful to try and extrapolate longer P2/P3 by only using the 100mg data, when its clearly the outlier vs 40-80mg groups.

Do I think there would be no WL difference in lager P2 between 40mg and 80mg? No, I’m sure we would see increased WL with increased dose. But it’s the 100mg 8.1% there’s the outlier.

I would also expect them to increase the dose to 125-150mg in longer P2 trials that gives possibility to do less aggressive titrating. SC VK2735 dosed up to 10mg in 4w P1, and up to 15mg in 13w P2. (we saw the exact same with Tirzpeatide )

While I am not blown away by the actual WL curve, I’m more excited over the trendlines from end of dosing (day 28) to end of trial (day 57) Those data is relative consistent through the different doses and show only minor weight gain.

They also did one cohort with 60/80mg where they from w3 dosed every second day. And the WL curve almost looks identical to the 60/80mg cohort with daily dosing through the entire 4w.

It’s still early days and with very few patients in a short trial. So, we shouldn’t conclude anything firmly on these data. But those data certainly look interesting. And VKTX already confirmed they will do one/more arms in the coming P2 with infrequently dosing.

Side effect.

Side effect from the 3 new cohorts seems to confirm the overall picture of very good tolerability (class leading) If this is confirmed in larger P2/P3 then vk2735 definitely have an advantage there. Especially in SC where we see about 30% dropout in the first 8-12w with wegovy and zepbound.

All in all, it was good oral vk2735 data, and that should definitely be seen later today when Nasdaq opens. But I also think there might be an overreaction, with the possibility to do some great trading for those who do that.

Despite the celebrity status “miracle” weight loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy have gained recently, it appears most Americans are not jumping at the chance to use them. A recent national survey found people strongly opposed using injectable weight loss drugs instead of making a diet change.

The survey by the Consult for the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine included 2,205 adults who answered several questions related to weight loss. For example, when people read the statement, “If I wanted to lose weight, I would rather take an injectable weight-loss drug rather than make a diet change,” only 23% of Americans strongly agreed with that opinion. Meanwhile, 62% of survey respondents disagreed with the statement, and another 14% were uninterested because they did not want to lose weight. For those actively looking to shed extra weight, 73% still disagreed with using a weight loss injection.

“The new findings do not mean that Americans do not want to lose weight; rather, most would prefer to change their eating habits than inject a medication,” says Neal D. Barnard, president of the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine, in a media release.

When asked, “If a plant-based diet might cause significant weight loss, I would be interested in trying it, at least briefly,” two-thirds of survey respondents claimed they would be open to it. Among people who expressed interest in losing weight, 68% strongly agreed with the statement, while 32% strongly disagreed.

He started the company at the beginning of the year with Bill Ronkoski, a former GLG colleague, and Jon Zajac, a former engineering leader at Teamshares and HubSpot.

The problem AggKnowledge is trying to solve will be familiar to any professional who gets random calls and emails to verify employment, title, role, and subject expertise. Most of that info is either available online, has already been answered, or could be inferred with a high degree of confidence.

The issue is that most of these databases are both hopelessly out of date and not precise enough. This is a particularly big problem for expert networks which are trying to match clients with individuals with specialized knowledge.

AggKnowledge combines data feeds about people, companies, and expertise, with sophisticated entity matching powered by AI to enrich biographical information and filter out the noise.

Let’s say you are looking for a doctor who performs robotic shoulder arthroscopy using da Vinci surgical systems, and another who switched from prescribing primarily Ozempic to Wegovy. That isn’t likely to be on their CV, LinkedIn, or web profile, but AggKnowledge can pull this from data sources.

By including additional details, such as what a company does, its competitors, its size, revenue estimates, ownership information, and subsidiary structure it helps ensure the people you are reaching out to are appropriate matches.

Detailed biographical information would be helpful not just for expert networks and survey panels, but also companies hiring talent and organizations that are managing a community, such as universities reaching out to alumni.

Who Qualifies for Medicare-Covered Weight Loss Medicine?

A recent study investigates the impact of Medicare covering semaglutide for people with obesity and cardiovascular disease, exploring how many people could qualify based on different criteria.

+ Millions Could Benefit:
Millions of older Americans with obesity could soon receive Medicare assistance for weight-loss medication to reduce their risk of heart problems. Semaglutide, a weight-loss drug, is already approved for those with diabetes, but now Medicare covers it for people with obesity and cardiovascular disease without diabetes.

+ What Level of Cardiovascular Risk is Covered?
The study, led by Dr. Alexander Chaitoff from the University of Michigan, delves into who qualifies based on cardiovascular risk. If only people who have already had a heart attack or stroke qualify, about 3.6 million people would be eligible. If coverage expands to those at high cardiovascular risk (but without a major diagnosis), another 5.1 million could qualify. Adding those at moderate risk brings the total to 6.5 million.

+ How Much Will It Cost?
Depending on how many people Medicare covers, the costs could vary widely. For example, if only people with a history of heart attacks or strokes are eligible, and if 30% of them start using the drug, the first-year cost to Medicare could reach over $10 billion.

+ A Broader Look:
The study looked at data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey to calculate cardiovascular risk scores. This approach gives a better understanding of who is most at risk and how treatment can help prevent future heart issues.

+ What’s Next?
As more people could benefit from weight-loss medications like semaglutide, healthcare providers will need to determine which patients are eligible. Coverage decisions could have a huge impact on millions of Americans and potentially save lives.

+ Key Takeaways:
Medicare now covers semaglutide for some people with obesity and cardiovascular disease.
Between 3.6 million and 6.5 million Americans could qualify, depending on cardiovascular risk.
The cost to Medicare could exceed $10 billion, depending on how many people are covered.
The study highlights the need for clear guidelines on who qualifies for this coverage.

MAHA Idea #21 (9-27-24) (see prior posts for all my MAHA Ideas– numbering corrected because there were two #14s):  Stop funding Pharma R&D and profits for the entire world, in the form of higher prices.

Perhaps I’ll flesh out in a subsequent MAHA Idea regarding whether NIH should continue the ~$30B annually to fund research where pharmaco businesses capture the vast majority of any future profits, while the American taxpayer takes much of the risk. Today, however, I want to talk about prices.

First, let’s level-set on Ozempic and Wegovy, two of the fasted growing drugs in the world. Novo Nordisk (a Danish company) doesn’t disclose exactly how much revenue it has in the US for these two drugs, but it’s reasonable to assume based on public information that 2024 US revenue will be ~$50B, up from ~$30B in 2023. Looking at it per dose, Medicare pays ~$935 per month for Ozempic, whereas the National Health Service in the UK pays $140 per month and the drug costs <$100 per month in Germany. As a result, the US funds the vast majority of the revenue and profits of this particular Danish company. The US government has it within its power to negotiate those prices down for Medicare, especially after the recent legislation opening that door for insulin and other pricy drugs. So, why would we pay so much?  Primary answer, the previously discussed conflicts of interest as the revolving door of agency and congressional staffers spins continuously passing lawyers, consultants, academic researchers and executives in and out of industry. These folks are working with their friends and future employers in any negotiation. Any permanent regulatory fix has to address COIs first.

But why not just let the market work? Why do we even need government to negotiate or, in effect, set prices?  The challenge here is that the captured medical associations also participate in the largesse of the pharma industry. Speaking fees, going through the above revolving door, research and publishing support, etc. are standard fare. And these same medical associations have signed off on “best practices,” such as bariatric surgery and/or Ozempic for children between the ages of six and twelve. So, as an insurer whether private or public, you will end up paying for the drugs and treatments recommended by those “best practices.” By contrast, in Germany or the UK, they’ll simply make the decision, “Nope. Too expensive for us, so we won’t be covering the treatment for our residents.” The conflicts and the “best practices” make that harder in the US.

Also, in the case of private health insurers, your Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) requirements under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) effectively cap the portion of premiums insurers can retain for administration, marketing, and profits at 15%. So, the more drugs, procedures and other medical expenses rise, the more profit insurers are permitted to make, measured in dollars.  Even big corporate employers should not kid themselves as to their “partnership” with insurance companies and third-party administrators. Further restrictions in ACA and ERISA prevent any “discrimination” against the chronically ill in terms of coverage AND premium pricing, with limited exceptions for certain wellness behaviors like quitting smoking.  As a result, a healthy ~60 year-old employee, who eats a whole-food, low-carb diet and is in the <1% his age who are on zero medication, have a zero cardiac calcium score and have none of the five indicators of Metabolic Syndrome, pays the exact same premium for health insurance as a morbidly obese employee of the same age who has Type 2 Diabetes and has had major heart events. (I discussed some of these issues in MAHA Idea #6, and of course this is a hypothetical and I’m NOT bitter.)

Until we can fix these twisted government-induced incentive structures (which fix I strongly recommend), we likely will need the government to take some reasonable action to lower prices akin to what was done with insulin or in Europe, although I doubt we’ll ever have the leverage with the pharmacos that European countries have for the reasons described. Note that Novo Nordisk’s gross margin is ~85%, so there likely is some room to come down on price if there’s pressure to do so.

The high costs of Ozempic and Wegovy in the U.S. compared to other countries can be attributed to several factors:

Pricing Strategies: Pharmaceutical companies often set higher prices in the U.S. due to the lack of government regulation on drug prices. In contrast, many other countries have government agencies that negotiate or regulate drug prices1.
Insurance and Middlemen: The U.S. healthcare system involves multiple intermediaries, such as insurance companies and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), which can drive up costs. The CEO of Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, has pointed to these intermediaries as a reason for the high prices2.
Market Dynamics: The U.S. market is more willing to pay higher prices for new and innovative treatments, which can lead to higher list prices. Additionally, the U.S. accounts for a significant portion of the global sales for these drugs, giving companies less incentive to lower prices1.
Research and Development Costs: Pharmaceutical companies often justify higher prices in the U.S. by citing the need to recoup the substantial costs associated with research and development. However, this argument is less convincing when the same drugs are sold for much lower prices in other countries2.
For example, Ozempic costs around $969 per month in the U.S., while it is only $155 in Canada and $59 in Germany. Similarly, Wegovy costs $1,349 per month in the U.S., compared to $265 in Canada and $82 in the U.K.12.

It’s a complex issue with no easy solutions, but ongoing discussions and legislative efforts aim to address these disparities.

Bill would allow the FDA to fine individuals, companies up to $500,000 for posting false information online about Ozempic, Wegovy

Two U.S. senators are aiming to crack down on deceptive or misleading online promotion of weight-loss and other prescription drugs by telehealth firms and social-media influencers who profit from their posts.

New bipartisan legislation proposed by Sens. Dick Durbin (D., Ill.) and Mike Braun (R., Ind.) would authorize the Food and Drug Administration to warn and potentially impose costly fines on those who post false information online about medicines, or omit important information about a drug’s safety risks.

One impetus for the bill, according to a Senate aide, is the 2024 reporting by The Wall Street Journal about how social media has fueled demand for Ozempic and Wegovy from Novo Nordisk as well as other drugs used for weight loss. The Journal found that posts on platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and Instagram often omit information about difficult side effects, and that some influencers and companies profit from the posts.

As with company drug advertisements, social-media posts sponsored by drug manufacturers are required by the FDA to cite the risks. But the senators say there is a regulatory gap in FDA oversight when it comes to advertisements from telehealth companies and influencers if there isn’t an established relationship with a drug manufacturer.

Durbin and Braun earlier this year called on the FDA to take action against the marketing of prescription drugs on social media, citing a proliferation of dangerous and misleading content by telehealth companies. Their letter to the FDA commissioner cited findings from a Journal investigation published in 2022 about misleading ads by telehealth companies.

When faced with the criticism, some telehealth firms have said that they provide safety information to patients and have procedures to vet the accuracy of posts by influencers with whom they work.

The new bill, “Protecting Patients from Deceptive Drug Ads Online Act,” says too many social-media posts provide false information, omit key side effects, or fuel demand for medications that might not be appropriate for a patient.

The bill aims to give the FDA authority to require drugmakers to disclose payments to influencers to the federal Open Payments database, as they currently do with payments to physicians and other health providers.

The FDA would also have the authority to issue warning letters to influencers and telehealth companies for deceptive and misleading promotions. Those who don’t comply with the warning letters would face fines of up to $250,000 for the first violation in any three-year period, and up to $500,000 for each subsequent violation in any three-year period.

The FDA enforcement would apply to online posts that yield a payment to the influencer or telehealth firm and contain false statements, omit facts regarding a prescription drug, or fail to include traditional risk and side effect disclosures.

It would exempt certain statements that occur in the course of bona fide patient care or describe someone’s personal experience.

The cost of managing Type 1 diabetes can be substantial, involving various expenses beyond just insulin. Here's a breakdown based on the information available up to September 2024:

- **Insulin Costs**: Insulin, a critical component for Type 1 diabetes management, has seen its costs fluctuate. For instance, in the U.S., without insurance, insulin can cost up to $1,700 per year, but with legislative changes aimed at reducing costs, some individuals have reported significant reductions, like from $200-300 a month to $70 every 90 days for those with good insurance.

- **Overall Annual Costs**: The total estimated cost for managing Type 1 diabetes, including insulin, supplies, and other medical expenses, has been reported to range from $10,000 to $12,000 annually in some cases. This figure can vary widely based on individual health needs, insurance coverage, and the use of additional technologies like continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) or insulin pumps.

- **Out-of-Pocket Costs**: For individuals with insurance, out-of-pocket costs for adults with Type 1 diabetes have been estimated around $2,414 annually, considering insulin, diabetes-related supplies, and other services. This number can be lower or higher depending on the specifics of one's insurance plan, including deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.

- **Technological Aids**: The use of advanced technologies like CGMs, insulin pumps, or other devices adds to the cost. While these can improve management and quality of life, they also contribute significantly to the financial burden.

- **Indirect Costs**: Beyond direct medical expenses, there are indirect costs like productivity loss due to health management, potential disability, or even premature mortality, which are harder to quantify but add to the economic impact of diabetes.

- **Global Comparison**: Costs can differ dramatically by country due to healthcare systems and policies. For example, treatments like semaglutide, used for diabetes management, show a wide price range globally, indicating how national health policies affect individual costs.

- **Legislative and Advocacy Efforts**: There's been a push towards reducing these costs through legislation, as seen with efforts to cap insulin prices or provide broader coverage for diabetes management tools, which could eventually lower the financial burden for individuals.

Given this information, managing Type 1 diabetes involves not just the cost of insulin but a comprehensive array of expenses that can easily exceed $10,000 annually, even with insurance, due to supplies, technology, and other health-related costs. However, these figures can be significantly influenced by individual health needs, insurance specifics, and evolving healthcare policies aimed at reducing the financial strain on patients.

Who's paying for this research?

It seems like every week, there's a new headline about the health benefits of GLP-1s, the new class of injectable weight loss drugs like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy.

However, in a new editorial published in the Journal of Public Health Management and Practice, a group of public health specialists pointed out that the companies funding the research into these drugs and their safety are often the same ones making billions of dollars from their runaway popularity.

In their commentary, the Duke-led group of health researchers suggest that there's a glaring conflict of interest when companies like Novo Nordisk, the maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, initiate research into the safety and efficacy of these drugs.

As these experts point out, studies have shown that "clinical trials sponsored by pharmaceutical companies are more likely to yield favorable results for company products than independent trials."

This so-called "sponsorship bias" can not only lead to favorable academic papers, but similar boosterism in the media and public perception of the drugs. The trend is further complicated as both doctors and influencers are paid to push the injections without revealing negative side effects like gastrointestinal distress.

Along with recommending that organizations like the National Institutes of Health fund more objective research into the safety of these kinds of drugs, the researchers also said that social media posts about them should be "flagged and accompanied by accurate health information from reputable authorities" like the NIH or FDA — like that nearly three-quarters of patients taking semaglutide experienced gastrointestinal disorders like nausea and diarrhea.

At times, there seems to be tension in the commentary's takeaways: in addition to issues around potential bias, the researchers also criticize semaglutide's high cost, saying it makes the drug hard to access for the underserved communities who might need it most.

However, like all medications, it comes with a range of potential side effects and risks. Here's a comprehensive overview based on the information available up to August 2024:  1. **Gastrointestinal Issues**: These are among the most commonly reported side effects:    - Nausea and vomiting, which can be severe for some users.    - Diarrhea, which might be uncontrollable in some cases.    - Constipation due to delayed gastric emptying, which can lead to conditions like gastroparesis (stomach paralysis).  2. **Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar)**: Especially when combined with other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas. Symptoms include dizziness, confusion, sweating, and in severe cases, loss of consciousness.  3. **Kidney Injury**: There's a noted risk of kidney problems, although recent studies suggest Ozempic might reduce the risk of kidney failure in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease.  4. **Pancreatitis**: Characterized by severe abdominal pain that might radiate to the back, this is a serious but less common side effect.   5. **Thyroid Cancer**: There's a boxed warning regarding a potential increased risk of thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). This risk led to a contraindication in patients with a personal or family history of MTC or in patients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).  6. **Gallbladder Issues**: Including gallstones, which might be related to rapid weight loss rather than the drug directly.  7. **Allergic Reactions**: Can range from mild reactions like rash or itching to severe reactions like anaphylaxis, which requires immediate medical attention.  8. **Vision Changes**: Blurred vision can occur due to changes in blood sugar levels affecting the eye's lens.  9. **Cardiovascular Effects**: While Ozempic has been shown to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in some studies, individual reactions can vary, and there's always a potential for adverse cardiovascular effects in susceptible individuals.  10. **Mental Health**: Although less documented, there have been mentions of increased suicidal ideation or thoughts, though some data suggests a decrease in these thoughts compared to other weight loss medications.  11. **Weight Gain After Discontinuation**: While Ozempic can lead to weight loss, stopping the medication might result in weight regain.  12. **Injection Site Reactions**: Common with injectable medications, including pain, redness, or swelling at the site of injection.  13. **Potential for Abuse**: Given its off-label use for weight loss, there's a risk of misuse or over-reliance on the drug for cosmetic reasons rather than for its intended medical use.  14. **Long-term Effects**: As with any relatively new medication, long-term effects beyond what's currently known might still be emerging.  When considering Ozempic or any medication, it's crucial to weigh these risks against the benefits, particularly in the context of managing diabetes or other conditions for which it might be prescribed. Always consult with healthcare providers for personalized advice, considering individual health profiles, other medications, and lifestyle factors. Remember, while many experience side effects, not everyone will encounter all or even any of these risks, but awareness is key for informed decision-making.

There's a Danish company called Novo Nordisk, which makes semaglutide, the weight loss drugs Wegovy and Ozempic. This company is now the most expensive company in Europe, valued at $570 billion. That's more than the GDP of Denmark, where it's based.

What are your thoughts on this situation, and what does it tell us about the world we're living in?

It's crazy. Novo Nordisk is actually going to end up becoming the biggest company in the world. The market of overweight and obese people has barely been tapped by these companies. A recent study showed that only 12% of adults in the US have tried some kind of weight loss drug like semaglutide or tirzepatide, the competitor. There are a billion obese people in the world now, which is a huge captive market for these companies.

My fundamental problem with these weight loss drugs is that they're a band-aid for a broader problem. We're living in a way that is maladaptive. We've created a food system where human beings consume vast quantities of processed food, rather than the foods they should be eating. We've created a system where we're chronically stressed all the time, where we're constantly exposed to blue light. All sorts of other aspects of modern life are very maladaptive. And that's what's making us unwell.

Drugs like Ozempic allow that system to continue. They allow the situation to be perpetuated. You don't address the underlying problems. You don't try to make civilization better for human beings. There's a broader question of whether you actually can.

It's like, can you have a modern civilization that actually works for human beings? Because we've evolved for 200,000 years in hunter-gatherer societies. The modern world couldn't be more radically different from the environment in which we evolved if we tried. So there's a question of whether or not actually we can make the modern world better for human beings, but I think that we ought to try. And I think that using these drugs simply, like I say, is a band-aid.

It also affords much greater control, much more power to big pharma as well. This is another thing that I talk about.

For the longest period of time, control of a person's weight was their own problem. It was their own responsibility. It was the responsibility of their local community, of their family, etcetera. People were sort of enmeshed in a kind of food culture that placed limits on what people could eat and how they ate it, the particular circumstances in which they would eat, and that regulated people's weight. But now what we're seeing is that these companies are basically advocating for surrendering control of weight control to corporations.

That's what's interesting. They're really pushing this line that actually there's no element of personal responsibility in being overweight. None at all. You know, like, it's your genes, it's the environment, it's anything but you. There's no element of personal responsibility. So you can go on a diet, but it won't work. You can do exercise, but it probably won't work. You know, you're fat, because it's not your fault. Okay? It's kind of like having toenail fungus or something. It's a problem that just needs to be treated with a technical intervention, basically. And that's a drug, that's an injection or a pill.

And what that does then is that surrenders yet another aspect, yet another facet of our lives to big pharma, to control, affords them even greater power. So now we're not responsible for managing our weight. We need big pharma to do that in the same way that we're now not responsible for our moods. We need big pharma to do that. We need antidepressants, we need anti-anxiety drugs, etcetera.

I see it as part of a sort of broader creeping medicalization of society. And I think that it's very disabling for people. I don't think that being overweight or obese is necessarily just a matter of personal responsibility.

Some patients treated with semaglutide for diabetes or obesity have reported a reduced desire to smoke, raising the question of its potential benefit in tobacco use disorders (TUD).  To examine the association of semaglutide with TUD-related health care measures (medical encounter for diagnosis of TUD, smoking cessation medication prescriptions, and smoking cessation counseling) in patients with diabetes and TUD, this emulation target trial was conducted.  Electronic health records were utilized for a time period of December 2017 and March 2023 to identify patients with new use of semaglutide vs seven other diabetes medications (metformin, insulin, SGLT-2 inhibitors, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, other GLP-1 RA).  The primary outcome was TUD-related health care measures that occurred within a 12-month followup, which were examined using Cox proportional hazards and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.  Of the 222,942 new users of the eight medications, 5,967 were prescribed semaglutide.  Compared with the other medications, semaglutide was associated with a significantly lower risk for TUD diagnosis encounters.  This association was strongest for insulin (HR, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.63 to 0.74), and weakest but statistically significant compared to other GLP-1 RAs (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.81 to 0.96).  In addition, semaglutide was associated with fewer prescriptions for smoking cessation medications as well as counseling.  The findings were similar in patients with and without comorbid obesity.  The greatest differences occurred within 30 days of prescription initiation for most of the group comparisons.  The authors suggested that their findings be explored in further clinical trials to evaluate the potential role of semaglutide in supporting smoking cessation.  The limitations of this trial include residual confounding, documentation bias, missing data on current smoking behavior, BMI, and medication adherence.

Protein for Weight Loss: A Medical Perspective on Optimal Nutrition
As a medical professional specializing in weight management, I often discuss the crucial role of protein in achieving and maintaining a healthy weight. Many patients ask about the most effective strategies for weight loss, and consistently, protein emerges as a key factor in successful weight management programs.

Understanding Protein's Role in Your Body
Protein is an essential macronutrient composed of amino acids, which are fundamental building blocks for various bodily functions. These amino acids are crucial for muscle development, hormone production, and overall cellular health. When we consider weight loss, protein's importance becomes even more pronounced (1).

The Science Behind Protein and Weight Loss
Scientific research has consistently shown that increasing protein intake can significantly aid in weight loss efforts. Here's how protein contributes to effective weight management:
-Satiety Enhancement: Protein-rich foods promote a feeling of fullness, technically known as satiety. This increased satiety can lead to reduced overall calorie intake, a key factor in weight loss.
-Metabolic Boost: Consuming adequate protein helps preserve lean muscle mass during weight loss (2). This preservation of muscle tissue is crucial because muscle is metabolically active, meaning it burns more calories even at rest compared to fat tissue.
-Hormonal Regulation: Protein consumption affects various hormones related to hunger and fullness. It reduces levels of ghrelin, often called the "hunger hormone," while increasing levels of peptide YY and GLP-1, hormones associated with feeling satisfied after eating.

Optimal Protein Sources for Weight Loss
When advising patients on protein sources, I emphasize the importance of whole foods. Lean meats, fish, poultry, eggs, and dairy products are excellent animal-based protein sources. For those following a plant-based diet, legumes, quinoa, and soy products offer high-quality protein options.
While whole food sources are preferable, protein supplements can be beneficial in certain situations. Whey protein, for instance, is quickly absorbed and can be useful post-exercise. However, it's crucial to remember that supplements should complement, not replace, a balanced diet.

Implementing a Protein-Focused Weight Loss Plan
To effectively incorporate protein into your weight loss strategy, aim for a balanced distribution throughout the day. Including a source of protein with each meal can help maintain steady energy levels and control hunger.
A general guideline is to consume about 0.8 to 1 gram of protein per kilogram of body weight daily. However, during active weight loss, this requirement may increase. It's essential to consult with a healthcare provider or registered dietitian to determine the right amount for your individual needs.

The Holistic Approach to Weight Management
While protein is a crucial component of weight loss, it's important to remember that successful weight management involves a comprehensive approach. This includes:
-Calorie Control: Maintaining a calorie deficit is fundamental for weight loss.
-Balanced Nutrition: Incorporate a variety of nutrient-dense foods, including fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.
-Regular Physical Activity: Combine resistance training with cardiovascular exercise for optimal results.
Adequate Sleep and Stress Management: These factors play a significant role in weight regulation and overall health.

Conclusion: Protein as a Cornerstone of Effective Weight Loss
In my professional experience, incorporating adequate protein into a well-rounded weight loss plan can significantly improve outcomes. It supports muscle maintenance, enhances satiety, and contributes to overall metabolic health (3).
Remember, every individual's nutritional needs are unique. While this advice provides a general framework, it's crucial to consult with a healthcare professional before making significant changes to your diet or embarking on a new weight loss journey.
By focusing on protein-rich, whole foods and adopting a balanced approach to nutrition and lifestyle, you can create a sustainable path to achieving and maintaining your ideal weight.

DO GLP-1 Agonists Really Cause Eye Disease

There has been a huge amount of press about a report showing an association between the use of GLP-1 agonists and Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION)

https://t.co/IjBl0wN10a

Because of it being heavily promoted by JAMA, the article has an Altmetric score of 1982. However, despite wide dissemination of the study's conclusions, very few people actually read the article (only 3,918 downloads-consider the denominator here: 1 million physicians in the US and 10 million healthcare providers).

The conclusions should not be accepted without critical analysis of the study itself. There are limitations:

1) This disease occurs in patients with diabetes. GLP-1 drugs are generally used for more advanced cases of DM. There was no control for diabetes severity in the study. It is likely that the NAION was more likely to occur in patients with more severe DM - the same population more likely to be prescribed GLP-1 agonists. The lack of control for DM severity is a major limitation and probably should negate any conclusion about the relationship between GLP-1 agonists and eye disease.

Note form the limitations section: "our study also is
limited in that the severity of confounding factors could not be adequately assessed,"

At a minimum, this analysis should have controlled for HgA1c levels.

2) The study had an extremely small number of patients and the population was not representative of the average patient with DM. Of 979 eligible patients, only 32 had NAION. Of these 27 were treated with semaglutide and 5 with other drugs. Semaglutide is not a 1rst line treatment for DM. That the majority of patients in this study were being treated with this drug suggests that the patients had severe, probably poorly controlled DM. Note #1 above- the statistical analysis for this study did not include control for DM severity.

See: DM Standards of Care from the ADA: https://t.co/hFlR9wPj25
The first line treatment for DM is diet control, weight loss and metformin. GLP-1 agonist drugs are advised when these fails or if treating patients with a high risk for DM complications. 

2) From the methods: Propensity matching was used to assess whether prescribed semaglutide was associated with NAION in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) or overweight/obesity. Propensity methods do not balance unmeasured risk variables or confounders. They also result in loss of information and power by excluding patients who cannot be matched. In the study, there were 32 patients with a NAION event. Of these only 23 were studied after a propensity score match and 18 after propensity score and exact matching. How the excluded patients might affect the results is unknown. 

3) As mentioned in a previous tweet (X?), the confidence intervals for the study results were huge. This happens when there are too few events to reliably analyze. 

From the abstract:

"A Cox proportional hazards regression model showed higher risk of NAION for patients receiving semaglutide (hazard ratio [HR], 4.28; 95%CI, 1.62-11.29); P < .001)."

"A Cox proportional hazards regression model showed a higher risk of NAION for patients prescribed semaglutide (HR, 7.64; 95%CI, 2.21-26.36; P < .001)."

As a general rule, findings with very large confidence intervals should be considered suspect-In other words, there is not a lot of confidence in the results. 

The figure got a lot of attention. Note that the effect was magnified by an insert showing survival probabilities between 90 and 100. the figure looks dramatic because of this. this got the public's attention but is misleading. There are no confidence intervals in this graph to show how well separated the groups survival really was. Given the very small numbers of patients, the CIs probably showed significant overlap. 

The major problem here is that this research really does not show an association between NAION and GLP-1 drugs-Yet, it was widely summarized by the press and made its rounds through social media. It came to my attention when someone sent e the article suggesting that our group look at this problem in more detail. 

It would be nice if there was more critical review of findings like these before the public absorbed the conclusions. 

I am sure there is more to this article than I picked up on and look forward to more discussion about it. 

Social media is probably a better venue for peer review for scientific findings than journals-This comes from someone who was a JAMA editor for many years. SM enables broader audience to draw upon for comment and facilitates expression of a diversity of views.

While the reported relative risk reduction is significant, it's crucial to consider the absolute risk reduction to accurately assess the semaglutide's effectiveness and calculate the number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one adverse CVD event.

These principles can be used to look at how any drug should be used in healthcare system’s such as the UK’s NHS. What are the key considerations?

Relative vs. Absolute Risk Reduction:

Relative Risk Reduction (RRR): Indicates the percentage reduction in risk between the treatment group and the control group. This figure often appears more impressive (because it is larger than the absolute risk reduction) but doesn't provide the complete picture about a drug’s effectiveness or how it should be used in clinical practice.

Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR): Measures the actual difference in event rates between the treatment and control groups, offering a clearer view of the treatment's real-world impact.

Number Needed to Treat (NNT): NNT is derived from the ARR and indicates how many patients need to be treated to prevent one adverse event. It is calculated as NNT = 1/ARR
Lower NNT values indicate more effective treatments in the sense that fewer patients need to be treated to prevent one clinical event such as a heart attack, stroke or death.

Importance in Different Risk Populations:
High-risk patients often show more substantial absolute benefits from treatments. In lower-risk patients, the ARR might be smaller, leading to a larger NNT, which influences cost-effectiveness and decisions about resource allocation.

Cost-Effectiveness: Assessing the economic viability of semaglutide involves comparing the cost of the drug against the healthcare savings from prevented CVD events.

Health economics studies are essential to determine if the benefits justify the expense, particularly in public health systems with budget constraints.

Side Effects and Safety Profile: Understanding the adverse effects of semaglutide is critical. Extended Safety Profiles: Long-term studies to monitor side effects and overall safety, ensuring that the benefits outweigh the risks.

I am particularly enthusiastic about the use of medications targeting Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors. These medications, known as GLP-1 receptor agonists, have traditionally been used to treat type 2 diabetes by helping to regulate blood sugar levels. However, recent research has unveiled their potential to benefit patients beyond diabetes management and weight loss.
GLP-1 (Glucagon-Like Peptide-1) is a hormone that plays a crucial role in regulating blood sugar levels. Here are some of its benefits:
Stimulates insulin secretion: GLP-1 encourages the pancreas to release insulin in response to elevated blood sugar levels, which helps lower blood glucose levels.
Inhibits glucagon secretion: Glucagon is a hormone that raises blood sugar levels by promoting the release of glucose from the liver. GLP-1 suppresses the secretion of glucagon, thereby preventing excessive glucose production.
Slows gastric emptying: GLP-1 slows down the emptying of the stomach, which helps regulate the rate at which nutrients, including glucose, are absorbed into the bloodstream after a meal. This can contribute to better blood sugar control.
Promotes satiety: GLP-1 also acts on the brain to increase feelings of fullness or satiety, which can lead to reduced food intake and potential weight loss.
Cardiovascular benefits: There is evidence to suggest that GLP-1 may have protective effects on the cardiovascular system, such as reducing the risk of heart disease and stroke. Recent research has shown promising potential for GLP-1 receptor agonists in managing heart failure. Heart failure is a condition characterized by the heart's inability to pump blood effectively, leading to symptoms such as shortness of breath, fatigue, and fluid retention. GLP-1 receptor agonists have been found to have beneficial effects on the heart beyond their glucose-lowering properties. They may improve cardiac function, reduce inflammation, and decrease oxidative stress, all of which are important in the pathophysiology of heart failure. Clinical trials have demonstrated that GLP-1 receptor agonists can reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events, including heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death, in patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease. These findings suggest that GLP-1 receptor agonists may have broader cardioprotective effects beyond their glucose-lowering actions. Several ongoing clinical trials are investigating the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists specifically in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Early results suggest that these drugs may improve outcomes and quality of life in this patient population, although more research is needed to confirm these findings.
Neuroprotective effects: Some studies have suggested that GLP-1 may have neuroprotective properties, which could be beneficial in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the brain, leading to motor symptoms such as tremors, bradykinesia (slowness of movement), rigidity, and postural instability. Preclinical studies have shown that GLP-1 receptor agonists have neuroprotective effects in animal models of Parkinson's disease. These drugs may help protect dopaminergic neurons from degeneration and promote their survival, potentially slowing the progression of the disease. In addition to their neuroprotective effects, GLP-1 receptor agonists have been found to improve motor function and reduce motor symptoms in animal models of Parkinson's disease. These effects may be mediated through various mechanisms, including increased dopamine release and modulation of neurotransmitter systems involved in motor control. Several clinical trials have investigated the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with Parkinson's disease. While results have been mixed, some studies have reported improvements in motor symptoms, activities of daily living, and quality of life with GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment. However, larger and longer-term trials are needed to fully evaluate the potential benefits of these drugs in Parkinson's disease.

In summary, GLP-1 receptor agonists like Ozempic/ Wegovy and Mounjaro/Zepbound hold promise not only in the management of type 2 diabetes and weight loss but also in the treatment of heart failure and Parkinson's disease. Further research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms of action and optimize the use of these agents in these conditions. However, it's important to note that while I am excited about the potential benefits of GLP-1 receptor agonists, there are potential side effects associated with these medications. Like all medications, GLP-1 receptor agonists can cause adverse reactions in some individuals, including gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. - **Less Common but Serious Side Effects**:

 "No, Diet and Exercise Are Not Better Than Drugs for Obesity":

1. Misinterpretation of Long-term Efficacy:

The article's focus on the Look AHEAD trial's results at 4 and 8 years suggests that lifestyle interventions are inherently less effective than medication. 

However, the Look AHEAD study was not designed to compare directly with obesity medications but to assess the impact of intensive lifestyle intervention on cardiovascular outcomes. 

Furthermore, lifestyle changes can yield significant health benefits beyond weight loss, such as improved lipid profiles, blood pressure, and insulin sensitivity, which are not always captured by weight loss percentages alone.

2. Overlooking the Variability in Individual Response:

Human response to diet and exercise varies widely due to genetic, environmental, and behavioral factors. 

The article does not account for personalized approaches to lifestyle interventions which can be tailored to individual needs, potentially leading to better outcomes than the averaged data from broad studies suggest. 

Personalized nutrition and exercise plans can outperform a one-size-fits-all drug regimen for many people.

3. Neglecting the Holistic Health Benefits of Lifestyle Changes:

Diet and exercise offer comprehensive health benefits that extend beyond mere weight loss. 

Physical activity, for instance, improves cardiovascular health, mental health, bone density, and muscle mass, none of which are primary outcomes of obesity medications like semaglutide or tirzepatide. 

The argument for drugs being superior overlooks these benefits which are crucial for overall health longevity.

4. Ethical and Psychological Impact:

The psychological aspect of weight management is significantly downplayed. 

Medications might lead to a dependency on drugs for weight control, potentially undermining personal agency and self-esteem. 

Conversely, mastering diet and exercise can empower individuals, improve self-efficacy, and foster a sustainable relationship with one's body and food. 

This aspect is critical for long-term health management and is not addressed in the article.

5. Sustainability and Side Effects:

While medications might show superior short-term weight loss, they come with side effects like nausea, gastrointestinal issues, and potential long-term health risks which are not adequately discussed. 

Diet and exercise, when implemented correctly, do not carry these pharmaceutical risks. 

Moreover, the sustainability of weight loss with medications is questionable once medication is discontinued, as weight regain is common, echoing the sustainability issues seen in lifestyle interventions but with added health risks.

6. Economic and Health System Implications:

The article does not delve into the economic implications of widespread use of expensive medications for obesity. 

The cost-effectiveness over time, especially when compared to lifestyle interventions, which could be cheaper in the long run by preventing other health issues, is not considered. P

ublic health systems would face significant financial strain if medications were the primary treatment for obesity, potentially leading to increased healthcare costs for all.

7. Cultural and Societal Bias:

The narrative seems to lean into the cultural bias that equates health solely with weight loss, ignoring the broader spectrum of health. 

The focus on drugs might perpetuate the misconception that personal effort in diet and exercise is futile, potentially discouraging people from adopting healthier lifestyles which have benefits far beyond weight management.

8. Prevention vs. Treatment:

The article fails to differentiate between prevention and treatment of obesity. 

Diet and exercise are foundational in preventing obesity, especially in children and young adults, where medications are less ideal. 

Prevention reduces the need for more aggressive treatments later, an aspect crucial to public health but not highlighted in the argument for drugs.

In summary, while medications can be an effective tool for weight loss, the argument that they are unequivocally better than diet and exercise oversimplifies the complex nature of obesity management.

Common Side Effects of GLP-1 Medications & How to Manage Them 💊

GLP-1 receptor agonists (like Ozempic®, Wegovy®, and Victoza®) are effective for managing blood sugar and promoting weight loss, but they can cause side effects. Here are the most common ones and tips to help manage them:

1.Nausea 🤢
•Why it happens: GLP-1 slows stomach emptying, which can lead to nausea, especially when first starting or increasing the dose.
•What to do:
•Eat smaller, more frequent meals.
•Avoid greasy, spicy, or overly rich foods.
•Stick with bland foods like crackers, toast, or rice during flare-ups.
•The nausea often improves as your body adjusts.

2.Diarrhea or Constipation 🚽
•Why it happens: The medication changes gut motility.
•What to do:
•Stay hydrated by drinking plenty of water.
•Eat fiber-rich foods to regulate digestion.
•Over-the-counter remedies like loperamide (for diarrhea) or stool softeners (for constipation) may help.

3.Vomiting 🤮
•Why it happens: Often linked to nausea or overeating.
•What to do:
•Avoid large meals.
•Let your healthcare provider know if vomiting persists—they may adjust your dose.

4.Heartburn or Indigestion 🔥
•Why it happens: Slowed digestion can irritate the stomach lining.
•What to do:
•Avoid lying down right after eating.
•Limit acidic foods and beverages (e.g., coffee, citrus).
•Over-the-counter antacids may provide relief.

5.Injection Site Reactions 💉
•Why it happens: Local irritation at the injection site.
•What to do:
•Rotate injection sites with each dose.
•Use proper technique and ensure the skin is clean before injecting.

While side effects are common, they’re often temporary and manageable. If they persist or become severe, contact your healthcare provider—they may adjust your dose or recommend additional strategies.

GLP-1 agonists, like Ozempic, Wegovy, and others, have indeed been hailed for their effectiveness in managing type 2 diabetes and aiding in weight loss. However, like any medication, they come with potential side effects and risks:

1. **Gastrointestinal Issues**: The most commonly reported side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. These can be quite severe in some cases, leading to dehydration or requiring medical intervention.

2. **Pancreatitis**: There's an increased risk of pancreatitis, which is inflammation of the pancreas. Symptoms might include severe abdominal pain, which might radiate to the back, along with nausea and vomiting.

3. **Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar)**: Especially when combined with other diabetes medications like sulfonylureas or insulin, GLP-1 agonists can lead to low blood sugar, which if severe, can result in confusion, dizziness, and in extreme cases, loss of consciousness.

4. **Medullary Thyroid Cancer**: There's a warning associated with these drugs regarding a potential increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma. This has led to GLP-1 agonists not being recommended for those with a personal or family history of this cancer or multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

5. **Kidney Issues**: There have been reports of acute kidney injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing kidney problems or those who become dehydrated due to the gastrointestinal side effects.

6. **Gallbladder Disease**: Research has suggested an association between GLP-1 agonists and an increased risk of gallbladder or biliary diseases, including gallstones.

7. **Serious Gastrointestinal Adverse Events**: Recent studies have highlighted cases requiring hospitalization due to severe gastrointestinal issues like ileus (blockage or paralysis of the intestines), though these are less common.

8. **Allergic Reactions**: Though less common, there are reports of severe allergic reactions which might include symptoms like rash, itching, swelling, severe dizziness, or trouble breathing.

9. **Injection Site Reactions**: Since most GLP-1 agonists are delivered via injection, reactions at the injection site, including pain, redness, or swelling, can occur.

10. **Mental Health**: There have been anecdotal reports, though less scientifically established, of mood changes, including depression or suicidal ideation, though these might be linked more broadly to the stress of managing chronic conditions rather than directly to the medication.

11. **Potential for Over-reliance**: Given their effectiveness in weight loss, there's a concern about dependency, where individuals might rely on these medications long-term for weight management rather than adopting lifestyle changes.

The "dark side" of GLP-1 agonists largely revolves around these side effects, which, for the majority, might be manageable or temporary, but for some, could be severe or life-altering. It's crucial for anyone considering these drugs to have a thorough discussion with healthcare providers about the risks versus benefits tailored to their health profile. Additionally, ongoing monitoring and awareness of these potential side effects are necessary for those who start these medications.

The sentiment you're describing taps into a broader social dynamic often seen with innovations, especially in health and medicine. Here's an interesting perspective on why this scenario could indeed be seen as "funny" or at least ironic:

1. Skepticism of New Treatments: 

Historically, there's always been a skepticism towards new medical treatments. The more revolutionary they claim to be, the more suspicion they tend to attract. If Ozempic, or semaglutide, turns out to be largely beneficial without the severe side effects some fear, it would be a classic case of "the boy who cried wolf" in medical science.

2. Schadenfreude: 

There's a human tendency to find humor or satisfaction in the failure or the non-failure, in this case, of things that are overly hyped or criticized. If Ozempic's critics are waiting for a downfall that never comes, there might be a comedic element in their ongoing disappointment.

3. The Cycle of Medical Approval: 

Often, drugs go through a cycle of wonder drug > criticized drug > accepted drug. If Ozempic follows this path without significant long-term issues, it would validate those who advocate for a more measured approach to new treatments, emphasizing the need for long-term studies over immediate judgment.

4. Cultural Impact: 

The narrative around weight loss solutions often includes a moral component, where some believe there should be a 'price to pay' for what seems like an easy solution to a problem traditionally requiring lifestyle change. If Ozempic defies this expectation by being safe, it could challenge these moralistic views on health and body image, leading to a shift in cultural attitudes.

5. Innovation's Irony: 

There's an irony in how society treats innovation. We crave advancements but are equally eager to see them fail due to a mix of fear, envy, or the comfort of the status quo. If Ozempic proves its worth over time, it would highlight how initial resistance to medical advancements can often be more about human psychology than the science itself.

However, it's worth mentioning that the absence of known serious side effects now doesn't guarantee there won't be any discovered in the future. Many drugs have had long honeymoon periods. But, if in 20 years Ozempic is still standing strong without significant drawbacks, it would indeed be a testament to its developers' claims and perhaps a lesson in the cautious optimism that should greet all medical innovations. 

Remember, though, humor in this context would be quite subjective and might not be seen as funny by those who've experienced any negative effects, however rare they might be.

People taking the drug behind Novo Nordisk’s (NVO) popular Ozempic were found to report suicidal thoughts at a higher rate than people taking other drugs, according to a new study published Tuesday by JAMA Network Open.

The medication, semaglutide, is sold by the the Danish pharma giant in the United States as Ozempic for diabetes and Wegovy for weight loss. The study raises additional concerns over a possible link between highly-coveted diabetes and weight loss drugs like Ozempic and suicidal ideation.

Earlier this year, both the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency launched their own investigations into the issue. Both health regulators determined there was no link between popular weight loss drugs and suicidal thoughts.

At the time, the FDA added it could not definitively rule out that “a small risk may exist” and said it would continue monitoring for side effects.

In the new observational study, researchers analyzed adverse drug reactions tracked by a World Health Organization (WHO) database. The analysis found 107 reports of patients taking semaglutide who said they had suicidal thoughts. When compared with all the other drugs in the database, people taking semaglutide had a 45% higher risk of reported suicidal thoughts. The risk was even greater for people taking semaglutide and antidepressants.

However, when researchers excluded patients on antidepressants, the link disappeared. Additionally, patients on semaglutide had a lower rate of suicidal behaviors, like suicide attempts and self-injury, when compared with other drugs in the database.

Novo Nordisk (NVO) told STAT in a statement that “the known risks associated with use of these medicines are reflected in their current FDA- and EMA-approved product labeling.” The company also noted that the new study had limitations since it couldn’t control for outside variable like patients’ diagnoses and medical histories.

•Side effects: hypotension, electrolyte abnormalities, neurohormonal activation, and adverse kidney events.
•Loop diuretics indicate more severe disease and may have limited effectiveness in obesity-related HFpEF due to unique mechanisms of congestion.

New Approaches and Trials

•Potential Benefits of New Therapies:
•Sacubitril/valsartan, MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors have shown to reduce loop diuretic requirements.
•Obesity-related HFpEF presents additional challenges with higher filling pressures and diuretic resistance.

Semaglutide in HFpEF

•STEP-HFpEF and STEP-HFpEF DM Trials:
•Semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, improved body weight, HF symptoms, exercise function, and reduced HF events.
•The trials examined the effects of semaglutide on diuretic use in obesity-related HFpEF.

Study Findings

•Diuretic Use and Effects of Semaglutide:
•Higher loop diuretic doses at baseline were associated with worse HF symptoms and greater body mass.
•Semaglutide improved HF-related outcomes irrespective of baseline diuretic use.
•Greater reduction in diuretic dose and discontinuation rates with semaglutide compared to placebo.

•GLP-1RAs like semaglutide may have decongestive effects through renal and hemodynamic improvements.

Conclusion

•Semaglutide provides significant benefits in managing obesity-related HFpEF, with potential to reduce reliance on loop diuretics.
•The findings support broader implementation of semaglutide for improving HF health status, but further evidence is required for definitive guidelines.

Lose the Fat, Not the Muscle: A Comprehensive Look at Weight Loss and Muscle Preservation

By Dr. Leon Katz

Introduction

Weight loss is a significant achievement for many struggling with obesity, but it often comes with unintended consequences like muscle loss. Research shows that weight loss methods, whether through dieting, medication, or bariatric surgery, can result in a reduction of muscle mass. This article explores the impact of GLP-1 agonists like Semaglutide (Wegovy) and Tirzepatide (Zepbound) on muscle loss and offers strategies to mitigate these effects (1,3).

The Significance of Muscle Loss

Obese individuals typically have more muscle mass compared to their normal-weight counterparts. However, during weight loss, they tend to lose more muscle mass. This is particularly problematic for specific groups, including postmenopausal women, the elderly, athletes, and those with metabolic diseases (2). The loss of muscle mass can lead to:

•   Fractures: Reduced muscle mass increases the risk of falls and bone fractures.

•   Fatigue: Lower muscle mass contributes to overall weakness and decreased physical endurance.

•   Lower Bone Density: Muscle supports bone health; losing muscle can result in weaker bones.

•   Slower Metabolism: Muscle mass is a key factor in metabolic rate. Losing muscle can slow down metabolism, making it easier to regain weight.

Mitigating Muscle Loss

To minimize muscle loss during weight loss, consider the following strategies:

1  Resistance Exercise:

Engaging in regular resistance training can help preserve muscle mass. Exercises like weightlifting, bodyweight exercises, and resistance band workouts are beneficial.

Starting with a professional trainer can help you perform exercises safely and effectively.

2  Increased Protein Intake:

Consuming adequate protein supports muscle maintenance and growth. Aim for a balanced intake that supports muscle preservation without overloading the kidneys or affecting insulin sensitivity.

Consult with a nutritionist to determine the appropriate amount of protein for your needs.

Conclusion

Obesity poses significant health risks, and weight loss is crucial for improving overall health. However, it's essential to be mindful of the potential downsides, such as muscle loss. By combining resistance exercise with a balanced protein intake and seeking professional guidance, you can achieve weight loss goals while maintaining muscle mass and metabolic health.
